h1: The 7 Best Network Switches Under $200 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Network Switches Under $200: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 network switches under $200 scored on port speed, port count and VLAN management, from 5-port gigabit to 24-port and 10GbE.
summary: The TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 is the best network switch under $200 for most homes: eight 2.5-gigabit ports at $50 to $100. The TL-SG105S-M2 shrinks that to five ports for less. The NETGEAR GS308E adds managed features like VLANs, the 10GbE model serves fast NAS setups, and the TL-SG1024DE covers 24-port wiring closets.
intro: The usual advice on switches is to count ports and buy the cheapest. That works until the day you plug a fast NAS or a 2.5G router into a gigabit switch and every port quietly runs at a fraction of its potential. A switch is only as fast as its slowest port, so the speed rating matters at least as much as the port count.

So we ranked on port speed first, then count, then management. We reviewed seven switches under $200 from their listings, from a five-port gigabit unit under $25 to a 24-port model and a mixed 10GbE switch, and weighed what each lets you do with VLANs, mirroring and monitoring. Cat5e and Cat6 limits matter too, which the listings address for the 2.5G models.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2
products.verdict: Eight 2.5-gigabit ports for $50 to $100, enough for a modern home or small office.
products.description:
The TL-SG108S-M2 offers eight 2.5-gigabit ports, built for LAN parties, home entertainment and small offices. Its listing highlights an instant upgrade to 2.5 Gbps without needing to move up to Cat6 cabling.

It ranks first because 2.5G is the sweet spot now: it matches modern routers, NAS boxes and Wi-Fi 6 access points, and eight ports cover most homes. Against the five-port TL-SG105S-M2 it gives three more ports for $50 to $100 instead of $25 to $50. It beats the gigabit units on speed at a similar price.

Buy it for a home or small office with a 2.5G router or NAS. The caveat: it is unmanaged, so there are no VLANs or traffic rules.
products.idealFor: Homes and small offices with 2.5G devices.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2
products.verdict: Five 2.5-gigabit ports at $25 to $50 for a desk or media cabinet.
products.description:
The TL-SG105S-M2 gives five 2.5-gigabit ports and the same promise as its larger sibling: instant 2.5 Gbps without Cat6 upgrades. It is built for LAN parties, home entertainment and small offices.

It ranks second because the eight-port TL-SG108S-M2 leaves more room to grow for $25 or so more. This five-port model is the better fit for a TV cabinet or a desk with a router, a PC, a NAS and a console, where you will never use eight ports.

Choose it for a small, speed-first setup. The caveat: five ports fill quickly, and one will be consumed by the uplink to your router.
products.idealFor: Desks and media cabinets with a handful of devices.
products.skipIf: You expect to add more wired devices.

products.name: NETGEAR 8-Port Gigabit Ethernet Easy Smart Managed Network Switch (GS308E)
products.verdict: Eight gigabit ports with a browser-based GUI and real traffic segmentation tools.
products.description:
NETGEAR's GS308E is an eight-port gigabit switch with an Easy Smart web GUI that works on Windows, Mac or Linux. The firmware handles VLANs (up to 64), QoS, IGMP snooping and port mirroring, tools that stop voice and video traffic being starved.

It ranks third because 1 Gbps ports trail the 2.5G models on speed, but it is the only managed option under $50 here. VLANs matter if you want to isolate IoT devices or guests from your main network. Against the TP-Link 8-port, it is simpler to configure.

Buy it if you need segmentation. The caveat: the web interface is simple, not enterprise-grade, so advanced routing needs better hardware.

keySpecs.label: Interface
keySpecs.value: Web GUI on Windows, Mac, Linux

products.idealFor: Homes that want IoT or guest network separation.

products.name: 10Gbe Ethernet Switch Unmanaged with 2 x 10Gb RJ45 Ports + 4 x 2.5Gb Base-T
products.verdict: Two 10Gb RJ45 ports plus four 2.5Gb ports in an unmanaged, plug-and-play switch.
products.description:
This unmanaged switch pairs two 10Gb RJ45 ports with four 2.5Gb Base-T ports. The listing claims 2.5 times the speed of standard gigabit and easy setup. The 10Gb ports are meant for a NAS, a workstation or an uplink to another switch.

It ranks fourth because six ports total is small and it is unmanaged, with no VLANs. It is the only option here that reaches 10G, which makes it the right choice if your NAS or video workstation can use it. At $50 to $100 it costs the same as the eight-port 2.5G model.

Buy it for fast storage and editing. The caveat: the 10G ports need devices and cables that support them, and the unbranded listing offers little support information.
products.idealFor: NAS and video-editing setups that can use 10G.
products.skipIf: You need many ports or management.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG1024DE
products.verdict: Twenty-four gigabit ports with jumbo frames and port mirroring for $50 to $100.
products.description:
The TL-SG1024DE puts 24 gigabit ports in one box, with 9k jumbo frame support for faster large file transfers and port mirroring for monitoring. That is rack-room capacity for a price under $100.

It ranks fifth because gigabit is slower than the 2.5G picks, and most homes will never fill 24 ports. It earns a place for structured wiring, where every room has a wall jack and the switch is the hub. Against the GS308E it offers triple the ports and fewer managed features.

Choose it for a wired house or a small office. The caveat: a 24-port switch is larger and may need a rack or shelf, and its fan or ventilation needs are not described.
products.idealFor: Structured wiring and small offices with many wired drops.
products.skipIf: You only have a handful of wired devices.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG116
products.verdict: Sixteen 10/100/1000 ports that are energy efficient, reliable and quiet.
products.description:
The TL-SG116 expands a network with 16 gigabit ports, energy-efficient technology and IEEE 802.3x flow control. The listing describes it as reliable and quiet, which matters when the switch sits in a living area.

It ranks sixth because the 24-port model gives more ports for the same $50 to $100, and the 2.5G units give more speed. The 16-port size is its niche: more than a home needs but smaller than a rack unit.

Buy it for a growing home lab or a wired office. The caveat: it is unmanaged, so it cannot separate traffic, and it tops out at gigabit speed.
products.idealFor: Home labs and offices that need more than eight ports.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105
products.verdict: Five gigabit ports, fanless and energy efficient, for under $25.
products.description:
The TL-SG105 offers five 10/100/1000 ports with auto negotiation, flow control, energy-efficient technology and a fanless design, all for under $25. Fanless means it runs silently.

It ranks last because the 2.5G TL-SG105S-M2 gives faster ports for $25 to $50 and most new gear can use them. The TL-SG105 remains the cheapest dependable way to add ports to a router, and it suits older networks where every device is gigabit.

Buy it for a simple desk or TV setup. The caveat: five ports at gigabit speed limit future upgrades, so choose the 2.5G model if you are planning a faster network.
products.idealFor: Simple desks and TV cabinets on a tight budget.

whatMatters.detail: Port speed is how fast each socket can move data: 1 Gbps, 2.5 Gbps or 10 Gbps. A fast NAS plugged into a gigabit port is capped at gigabit. 2.5G switches can use existing Cat5e cable over short runs. Check the speed per port in the title, and match it to your router and NAS.

Unmanaged switches work out of the box with no settings. Managed switches add VLANs, QoS and monitoring through a web interface. The NETGEAR GS308E lists up to 64 VLANs. You only need management to separate guest, IoT or work traffic. Otherwise, unmanaged is simpler and cheaper.

One port always connects the switch back to the router, so a five-port switch leaves four usable. Count your devices now, then add a few for growth. Eight ports suits most homes, sixteen or twenty-four suits structured wiring. Buying larger rarely costs much more.

Jumbo frames carry more data per packet, which helps large transfers between servers and NAS boxes. Flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. The TL-SG1024DE lists 9k jumbo frames and the TL-SG116 lists 802.3x flow control. Most home users never need to tune either.

Fanless switches use passive cooling, so they make no noise and have no part to wear out. That matters in living rooms and bedrooms. Many small switches are fanless, such as the TL-SG105. Larger 24-port units may use ventilation, so check the listing if silence is essential.

faq.q: Do I need Cat6 cable for a 2.5G switch?
faq.a: TP-Link says the TL-SG108S-M2 and TL-SG105S-M2 upgrade to 2.5 Gbps without needing Cat6, so Cat5e usually works over typical home runs. For 10G ports on the 10GbE switch, better cabling is wise.

faq.q: What is the most common switch mistake?
faq.a: Buying gigabit and plugging in a faster NAS. The switch then caps every port at 1 Gbps. If your NAS or router has 2.5G, choose the TL-SG108S-M2 or the 10GbE model instead of a TL-SG105.

faq.q: Is a managed switch worth it for home use?
faq.a: Only if you need VLANs. The NETGEAR GS308E lets you separate IoT devices from computers, which is a real security benefit. For plain connectivity, an unmanaged TL-SG108S-M2 is simpler.

faq.q: How do I set up a network switch?
faq.a: Plug power in, connect one port to your router, and plug in devices. Unmanaged models like the TL-SG105 need nothing else. For the GS308E, use the web GUI to set VLANs after the first boot.

faq.q: How do I maintain a switch?
faq.a: Keep vents clear, dust it occasionally and avoid stacking heat-producing gear on top. Fanless units like the TL-SG105 are low maintenance. For managed models, check for firmware updates once or twice a year.

faq.q: Can a switch speed up my internet?
faq.a: No. A switch adds ports and local speed, not internet bandwidth. It helps transfers between your own devices, such as a PC and NAS over 2.5G, but your internet plan still sets the connection to the web.

finalTake: The TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 is the best network switch under $200 for most homes, with eight 2.5G ports at a modest price. Choose the TL-SG105S-M2 for a small desk, the NETGEAR GS308E if you need VLANs, and the 10GbE switch for a fast NAS. Pay for speed only if your devices can use it.
